sentences.text: Parvicursor was a very small alvarezsaurid dinosaur that lived in Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous.
This animal possessed long, slender legs adapted for fast running, while its forelimbs were short and stubby with hands reduced to a single large claw.
Researchers suggest this unique claw may have been used for digging or opening termite mounds.
In 2022, scientists concluded that the holotype specimen—the specific fossil the species is based on—represents a juvenile individual rather than an adult.
The single large claw was likely not used for defense because of its short length and lack of flexibility.
The holotype specimen was discovered in 1992 and formally described in 1996.
A second species, Parvicursor remotus, is known only from an incomplete skeleton consisting mostly of the pelvis and hind limb.
Parvicursor is classified in the alvarezsaurid subfamily Parvicursorinae, alongside close relatives such as Shuvuuia and Mononykus.
Fossils were found in the Barun Goyot Formation of Khulsan, Mongolia, dating to approximately 72 million years ago.
The time range for Parvicursor is the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether there is a second, yet-unnamed, species of Parvicursor.
Researchers have suggested that the genera Linhenykus and Ceratonykus may be junior synonyms of Parvicursor.
